episodes.212837: Slightly higher moisture behind a backdoor front combined with intense daytime heating on June 18th resulting in the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms across the higher terrain during the afternoon and early evening hours. One thunderstorm near Abo and Mountainair produced a wet microburst induced severe wind gust at a personal weather station on the Dear Canyon Preserve. Higher moisture remained in place along and east of the central mountain chain on June 19th resulting in another round of scattered thunderstorms across the central mountain chain and adjacent highlands during the afternoon hours. Severe thunderstorms dropped large hail in San Jose, produced a wet microburst induced severe wind gust northeast of Vaughn, and severe wind gusts near Tolar. Thunderstorms tapered off around sunset both days due to the loss of daytime heating.
episodes.212946: A persistent and highly moisture-laden tropical pattern set the stage for the flash flooding event from June 19-21. Thunderstorms initially developed along the Sierra Madre Oriental and crossed into South Texas on June 19, encountering an environment characterized by extremely high precipitable water values of 2.2-2.5+ inches, extreme instability with CAPE often exceeding 2,500-4,500 J/kg, and weak steering winds. As a stubborn upper-level closed low became established over South Texas, deep tropical moisture continued streaming inland on persistent southeast to east onshore flow. Multiple outflow boundaries, a mid-level vorticity maximum, and the sea breeze provided repeated lifting mechanisms for thunderstorm development. With storm motions generally under 10-15 kt and low-level inflow often stronger than the steering flow, thunderstorms repeatedly back-built, trained, and regenerated over the same locations. Rainfall rates of 2-3+ inches per hour became common, while saturated soils from prior heavy rainfall further reduced infiltration capacity. The combination of near-record atmospheric moisture, slow-moving and training thunderstorms, and several rounds of convection associated with the stationary upper low ultimately led to widespread flash flooding concerns across South Texas and the Coastal Bend through June 21.
episodes.213158: Moisture associated with Tropical Storm Arthur approached Central Alabama on June 17 into June 18. On June 17, several showers and low-topped supercells developed over southeastern Central Alabama. One cell produced a well-defined funnel cloud in southeastern Lowndes County that was caught in at least two videos posted to social media. The next day, heavy rainfall near Chalkville led to a portion of Sweeny Hollow Rd being flooded.||In the wake of the remnants of Arthur passing through Central Alabama on June 18, a cold front entered the area and became stalled. On June 19, heavy rainfall became concentrated along a boundary along and south of the U.S. 80 corridor, leading to flooding issues in Pike and Lowndes counties. By June 20, the stalled front over Central Alabama reignited training thunderstorms along the U.S. 280 and I-22 corridors, with heavy rainfall of 2 to 5 inches causing flash flooding in the Birmingham metro area during the afternoon hours.
episodes.213273: Late on the night of June 18, coverage of showers and thunderstorms expanded in association with a cold front and a slow-moving shortwave trough. This system then pushed south through North Texas early the morning of June 19. As the front continued southward and the shortwave propagated eastward, a second round of showers and storms developed across Central Texas on Saturday, June 20. The primary hazard accompanying these storms was flash flooding, though a few instances of damaging winds were also reported.
episodes.213308: The combination of light winds and abundant tropical moisture made the atmosphere favorable for the development of weak tropical funnels. Most of these funnel clouds are short lived and usually do not touch the ground. However, if a tropical funnel touches down it is considered a tornado which happened briefly during late morning on June 20th.
episodes.213457: A line of thunderstorms pushed southeastward across central Kansas and the Flint Hills during the evening hours of June 19. These storms produced up to quarter size hail and 75 mph winds.
episodes.213670: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Wyoming as a strong cold front moved across the state. Several areas had multiple lines move through the same region during the event. Severe Thunderstorm Watch was in effect for most of the afternoon through the late evening hours.
episodes.213851: A trough pattern moved into the area on the 18th and 19th. On the 19th, a cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms produced widespread lightning (over 2500 strikes), heavy rainfall of 1 to over 2 inches and several reports of flash flooding in western NV from Stagecoach to southeast Reno/Hidden Valley, east Sparks to Lockwood and Spanish Springs. Hail up to 1��� diameter and wind gusts of 60-75+ mph also occurred with these storms as they pushed across northwest and west central NV.
episodes.213941: During the afternoon and evening hours of June 20, 2026, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked into eastern Nebraska, driven by increasing moisture transport and large-scale forcing for ascent. The greatest instability resided across southeast Nebraska, where radar interpretation noted the strongest hail cores through the evening. At 4:41 PM CST, the public reported quarter-sized hail (1.00 inch in diameter) near Jansen, Nebraska. The storms gradually pushed eastward and decayed later into the evening.
episodes.214009: A frontal boundary dropping southward on the 19th of June, combined with both weak upper level support with a mid level trough of low pressure and remnant moisture from Post Tropical Cyclone Arthur moving across the area from the Gulf Coast, resulted in widespread showers and thunderstorms across the JAX CWA. Isolated thunderstorm damage occurred, however the primary impacts to the region was areas of flooding due to very heavy rainfall.
episodes.214169: Isolated flash flooding occurred across portions of Southeast Texas.
episodes.214172: Storms produced strong winds over the Southeast Texas bays.
episodes.214468: Thunderstorms tracked across eastern Colorado during the afternoon and evening hours of the 20th. A couple of the storms became severe with hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter.
episodes.214547: A mid-level low pressure system associated with Post-Tropical Storm Arthur pushed slowly through the area resulting in several rounds of thunderstorms over the coastal waters.  Some of these storms produced strong downburst winds over the waters resulting in several marine thunderstorm wind events.
episodes.214551: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
episodes.214562: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in a few tornadoes affecting coastal Mississippi.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  A bow echo also developed over coastal Mississippi leading to severe winds and thunderstorm wind damage in the Gulfport-Biloxi metro area.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of coastal Mississippi including the city of Picayune.  Two fatalities occurred near Picayune where rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and QPE of 10 to 15 inches was noted.  This very high rainfall total resulted in major flooding on the West Hobolochitto Creek on June 18th and this is where the fatalities occurred.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 20th.  This activity was focused in Biloxi where additional flash flooding occurred.
episodes.214661: A typical summertime pattern produced scattered afternoon showers and thunderstorms with occasional severe weather reported.
episodes.214698: A weak cold front working across Ohio on the afternoon of June 20th resulted in one instance of severe strength wind gusts in Washington County. This brought down multiple trees in the Lowell township before departing to the east-southeast for the rest of the day.
episodes.214976: A weak surface frontal boundary stalled out over portions of Deep East Texas, Lower Toledo Bend Country, and into North-central and Northeast Louisiana during the early morning hours on June 20th, separating warm and very moist air near and south of the front from the slightly drier air to the north. A weak upper level disturbance traversed east atop the front throughout the morning through the early afternoon hours, which enhanced large scale forcing for the development of showers and thunderstorms containing heavy rainfall. As this continued through the morning, the periods of heavy rain moved repeatedly over the same areas, which resulted in widespread amounts of 2-6+ inches falling over Deep East Texas, Central and Northeast Louisiana. This produced multiple reports of flash flooding across these areas before the storms weakened during the afternoon.||The following are storm total rainfall amounts across portions of North Louisiana: ||Desoto Parish: 4 miles northeast of Pleasant Hill: 4.78 inches.|Red River Parish: 2 miles south-southwest of Coushatta: 4.02 inches, 1 mile west-northwest of Hall Summit: 7.38 inches.|Lincoln Parish: Ruston: 4.21 inches, 1 mile North of Ruston: 5.07 inches.|Jackson Parish: 7 miles west-southwest of Chatham: 4.75 inches, 3 miles south-southwest of Jonesboro: 4.00 inches.|Ouachita Parish: 8 miles Southeast of Downsville: 4.58 inches, 7 miles west-southwest of Claiborne: 4.60 inches.
episodes.214978: A weak surface frontal boundary stalled out over portions of Deep East Texas, Lower Toledo Bend Country, and into North-central and Northeast Louisiana during the early morning hours on June 20th, separating warm and very moist air near and south of the front from the slightly drier air to the north. A weak upper level disturbance traversed east atop the front throughout the morning through the early afternoon hours, which enhanced large scale forcing for the development of showers and thunderstorms containing heavy rainfall. As this continued through the morning, the periods of heavy rain moved repeatedly over the same areas, which resulted in widespread amounts of 2-6+ inches falling over Southern Cherokee County Texas, as well as other portions of Deep East Texas, Central and Northeast Louisiana. ||Although no flooding was officially reported, here are storm total rainfall amounts that were measured from various stations in Southern Cherokee County: ||7 miles southwest of Alto: 6.06 inches (HADS gauge along Highway 21 southwest of Alto along the Neches River at the Houston County line).|6 miles west of Alto: 6.01 inches (Located just off CR 2325 near Highway 294).
episodes.215068: Storms that developed produced wind gusts across Campbell county.
episodes.215091: A weak cold front moved into a warm, moist airmass over South-Central Texas and generated thunderstorms. Some of these storms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding.
episodes.215217: A few isolated to scattered thunderstorm moved east to southeast across far southwest Nebraska during the afternoon hours on the 20th, ahead of deepening High Plains low pressure. Hail up to three-inches in diameter occurred in Hitchcock county, and winds up to 60 mph occurred in Dundy county.
episodes.215221: A few isolated thunderstorms moved east across Yuma county during the afternoon hours on the 20th, ahead of deepening High Plains low pressure. Hail up to golfball size and winds to 66 mph were reported across the county.
episodes.215224: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
episodes.215270: An upper level shortwave moved over Wyoming, accompanied by a jet streak. The surface dew points remained low, resulting in large dew point depressions. The result was many severe thunderstorms that produced wind gusts in excess of 58 mph.
episodes.215552: Shortwave ascent and forcing out ahead of a cold front supported scattered thunderstorms in northwestern Pennsylvania in the afternoon hours. Sufficient MLCAPE values of 500-1000 J/kg and 30-40 knots of effective shear supported a few instances of tree damage.
episodes.215725: During the evening hours on June 19th, a couple of severe storms produced large hail, damaging wind gusts and two brief tornadoes. One of these storms trekked through Trempealeau County where it produced golf ball sized hail in Osseo as well as a weak EF-0 tornado which resulted in minor damage. An additional tornado was documented in Jackson County, but no damage was verified which resulted in an EF-U rating.
episodes.215733: Morning convection within deep layer south to southwest flow produced a waterspout over Gasparilla Sound in Charlotte County.
episodes.215773: Enhanced westerly flow with multiple embedded shortwave troughs brought scattered severe weather to northern Utah on June 20, 2026.
episodes.215802: Diurnal convection interacted with a very moist atmosphere across portions of Louisiana. These slow moving storms produced flooding and a report of damage.
episodes.215864: Additional heavy rainfall along with wet antecedent conditions lead to more flash flooding, some significant, in the Pine Belt region of Mississippi. Several major roads were flooded, as well as homes. Water rescues were conducted in the Seminary area as several cars became stranded.
episodes.215913: Thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts along the Space and Treasure Coasts.
episodes.215930: An upper-level disturbance permitted an unsettled weather pattern to remain over South Florida and the nearby waters for a portion of late June 2026.
episodes.215959: Some severe thunderstorm outflow winds occurred.
